notes.58: 77 is damaged (aue..er...ich); only 'hang' can be read. 85 sich întete is read as 'disguised himself'; uncertain. 98 dâ bevore hê reit is obscure: 'as he had ridden before'.
notes.1: 'iz' (it) in lines 2-7 refers to Merlin as a child (neuter kint). Line 3: 'zuo vollentagen' read as 'zuo vollen tagen', 'of full age', with 'ob' as 'as if'; uncertain. Line 8: 'verschiet' taken as 'passed (his days)'; the sense is uncertain. Line 19: 'en' read as the Ripuarian pronoun 'them', not a negative.

nodes.text: and so wise were his deeds
it wanted to direct all the counsel
as if it were of full age
No one heard it say
anything that was a lie
yet people often tormented it sorely
to make it tell lies.
He passed from those days in such a way
that he, Merlin, neither lied nor did wrong
in any kind of place.
Save that he was a child, he was [full] of skill.
He was long unchristened;
then he wished gladly to be a Christian.
That was done for him, and he was named Merlin.
When he came of age,
at times this one or that bade him tell
what was to happen to him;
he would not shrink from it out of fear;
he always told them the truth.
If any sorrow then befell them,
that was not his fault,
for Jesus Christ willed it.
Yet people blamed him for it often enough
and said many a rude thing to him.
He took it all in good patience.
Whenever he said anything, it came out exactly right.
They were then very glad to hear that,
and yet held it in mockery.
Whatever he said came to pass.
He cared little to see people;
he withdrew himself ever further from the world.
At last he grew so weary of them
who never had to do with a man.”
The steward came there
where he found Merlin.
He said, “Tell me, good Merlin,
what kind of end shall mine be?
Tell me too; you told it to all of them.”
Merlin said, “You will fall to your death.”
The steward did not like the speech;
it pleased him none too well.
Yet he spoke of it in mockery,
and thought to test it further.
He meant to go about it with cunning:
he let his beard grow
and changed his outer clothing;
he rode there on another horse;
he sought him until he found him.
Then he asked him at once
what kind of death his would be.
Then Merlin told him another:
“You shall [...] hang
before I am captured.”
The steward was pleased
that he had told him two deaths.
He rode home to tell it
to his friends as a lie,
as a thing that could never happen.
He said, “I shall look into it tomorrow.”
Again he disguised himself;
he went to Merlin about the matter
as though he had never seen him.
He said, “What will happen to me?”
“You will drown,” said Merlin.
He said, “How could that be?
Merlin, you always spoke the truth;
you have never yet lied;
now you have this third time
foretold me three kinds of death.
You are lying about two of them, Merlin.”
He said, “That may well please you.”
The steward was very cheerful;
he walked home, where before he had ridden,
and at once told all of it
to the king as a piece of trickery,
and to the whole household;
then they made sport of it.
After that, within a short time,
the steward was to ride
to the forest to hunt with the hounds.
When they began to run in full cry,
he hurried after; then his horse stumbled;
the lord fell downward;
down a high rock he fell;
the horse barely got back up.
A forked branch caught him by the feet;
his head hung into the water;
then he fell in and drowned.
The death was threefold, mixed together.
Because this had happened so to the steward,
the king trusted all the more
the words that Merlin spoke.
The king then had him sought;
what use was it that he was found?
